name: Insensitivity to Sample Size
description: People often treat results from small samples as if they were much more stable and representative than they really are. Low-N evidence feels cleaner and more reliable than sampling variability allows.
design_relevance_note: Directly relevant to usability testing, survey interpretation, experimentation, and dashboard readouts: teams can overgeneralize from five interviews, one small segment, or a short experiment window as if the signal were already settled.
prevalence_note: Common in experimentation, analytics, survey, and user-research practice because product teams constantly reason from small-N evidence, even if the full phrase is less famous than anchoring or loss aversion.

findings.description: People treated small samples as far more representative than statistical laws warrant, systematically underestimating sampling variability and overestimating how well low-N results should reproduce the properties of the larger population.
findings.source_title: Belief in the law of small numbers.

applications.title: Tversky & Kahneman's survey of professional psychologists' own statistical intuitions
applications.description: Surveying professional research psychologists about their own research decisions, Tversky and Kahneman found that most held an exaggerated belief in how likely a finding from a small initial sample was to replicate successfully -- treating a small, randomly drawn sample as far more representative of the true population than statistical theory justifies. The bias appeared even among the exact population (trained research scientists) one might expect to be immune to it, in the exact professional context (research replication judgment) where it has the most consequence.
applications.ethical_note: A foundational research-methodology finding with no persuasion or product-design dimension -- directly relevant to any team drawing product or design conclusions from small user-research or A/B-test samples, since the bias this study documents applies to exactly that kind of small-sample-to-general-conclusion reasoning.
